Q: Azure static webapp Oryx github build breaks A:

You can identify the exact cause of the failure by checking the GitHub Actions logs.

Go to your repository → Actions tab in GitHub → open the workflow run that failed (it will be marked in red).

Inside the failed job, expand the build logs generated by Azure Static Web Apps (Oryx build step).

In my case, the failure was clearly shown in the logs:

Treating warnings as errors because process.env.CI = true.

Failed to compile.

[eslint]
src/App.js
Line 2:8: 'logo' is defined but never used no-unused-vars

The issue was that:

import logo from './logo.svg';

Q: WPF lines and polylines events for a 2D Editor A:

In a 2D editor you actually don't want WPF to manage your geometry.

Most people start by putting Line, Polyline, etc. on a Canvas and trying to attach mouse events to them.

That works for a drawing demo, but it breaks down immediately once you need snapping, handles, zoom, or precise selection.

Treat WPF as a renderer only. All editor behavior should come from your own model + hit-testing.

1. Clicking a line / polyline

Do not rely on Shape.MouseDown or something.

Convert mouse position:

screen -> world coordinates

Then test against your geometry:

distance(point, segment) < tolerance

That is how CAD/diagram editors detect selection.

2.1 Detecting endpoints / showing small boxes

Endpoints are just another hit-test:

distance(point, segment.start) < tolerance
distance(point, segment.end) < tolerance

The small square/dot is not a WPF control. It is a selection handle drawn by the editor after selection.

2.2 "Near" events

Editors usually don't use events for this. They continuously hit-test during MouseMove and switch tool state:

Idle -> Hover -> Dragging -> Editing

Snapping and highlighting come from this loop.

3. Pan and zoom

Never move shapes. Move the camera.

Use a transform:

world -> view -> screen

Zoom = scale Pan = translation

4. Keeping aspect ratio

Use a single uniform scale factor for X and Y.

If X and Y scales differ, lengths visually change (circles become ellipses).

I ended up implementing this architecture in a small editor as a reference example, in case seeing the structure helps:

https://github.com/kehan-zhou/flux2d-editor

Q: How to checkout a branch when all branches are already checked out at '<current_working_tree>' A:

First, the modern command would be git switch --ignore-other-worktrees <your-branch>, instead of the old and obsolete git checkout command.

Second, in a more Docker-native setup, it is better to use Docker volumes or bind mounts to manage source code and data, rather than trying to manipulate Git repositories inside the container.

That way, you can keep the container's filesystem clean and focused on running the application, while the host manages the source code and version control.

Q: How can I override a property in a way that gives me static access to the property? A:

I'm not sure I follow your design, but I would probably not tie permissions to forms. A typical design is to have a database, application server, and application. Where the application server is something like a asp.net server or similar that accepts requests, checks permissions, and forwards valid requests to the database.

This has some advantages when managing permissions over using the database to do so. You can define permissions on higher level actions like "borrow book" and "return book" instead of lower level permissions like read/write access to tables or columns.

Even if you manage permissions in the application server you still want to configure the UI to hide or disable functions that are not allowed, but this is just a usability issue, not a security issue.

Q: What is the return type of a constructor in java? A:

At the JVM level, static initialisers and constructors are methods which return void. Static initialisers are static methods, however constructors use this and don't need to return anything. This is because the caller is responsible for creating the object (not the constructor).

If you try to only create an object in byte code without calling a constructor you get a VerifyError. However on the Oracle JVM you can use Unsafe.allocateInstance() to create an object without calling a constructor,

The static initialiser is called <cinit> which takes no arguments and the constructor is called <init>. Both have a void return type.

For the most part, this is hidden from the Java developer (unless they are generating byte code), and the only time you see these "methods" in stack traces (though you can't see a return type).
